passage: In the village near Hassan, Siddharth had started giving his son Pradeep a one-rupee coin for every chore during the summer holidays. It worked at first: the calves got water, the hens got grain. But by the end of May, when Siddharth asked Pradeep to shut the gate before the goats wandered, the boy stood still and asked, "How much?" The goats were already halfway to the road. That night Siddharth sat on the verandah, thinking. The next morning he didn't mention coins. When Pradeep carried the bucket to the calves, Siddharth said, "Look how fast the small one drinks. She waits for you now." Pradeep grinned and went back for a second bucket without asking anything.

qa.q: What did Pradeep ask when told to shut the gate?
qa.a: The boy stood still and asked, "How much?"

qa.q: What might Siddharth have been thinking on the verandah that night?
qa.a: He was probably worried that the coins had turned helping into a trade, since the goats wandered while Pradeep waited to hear the price.

qa.q: What did Siddharth choose to do the next morning, and what effect did it have?
qa.a: He dropped the coins and pointed out that the small calf now waits for Pradeep, and the boy fetched a second bucket without asking.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel when told the calf waits for him?
qa.a: Pradeep probably feels proud and needed, which gives the chore a reason bigger than a coin 😊.

grounding: A young father sees coins make his son ask 'how much' before chores and switches to noticing what the work means.

passage: In their small apartment in Busan, Soo-ah had praised her daughter Leila constantly: "Amazing! Genius! Here's a sticker!" for every drawing, every tidy shelf. One evening Soo-ah asked her to set out the spoons for dinner. Leila folded her arms. "Do I get a sticker?" Soo-ah paused with the rice pot. She realised Leila hadn't set the table without a sticker in weeks. That night she put the sticker sheet in a drawer. The next evening, when Leila laid the spoons out, Soo-ah said, "You put Halmeoni's spoon near her tea, because her hands shake. That was thoughtful." Leila looked at her grandmother's place, then quietly straightened the spoon again.

qa.q: Where did Leila put Halmeoni's spoon?
qa.a: Near her tea, because her hands shake.

qa.q: What did Soo-ah realise as she paused with the rice pot?
qa.a: She realised constant praise and stickers had made Leila expect a prize for every small job, which worried her.

qa.q: Which kind of praise did Soo-ah switch to, and why might it last longer?
qa.a: She named the thoughtful thing Leila did for Halmeoni, linking the task to caring for someone instead of to a sticker.

qa.q: What might Halmeoni notice when Leila straightens the spoon?
qa.a: Halmeoni may see her granddaughter taking care over her needs for their own sake, which feels warmer than a chore done for a sticker.

grounding: A mother notices her daughter asking for a sticker before chores and shifts to naming the meaning of her effort.

passage:
At the Saturday gardening club in the community centre, the coordinator handed each child a small watering can. Yogesh, six, didn't move. 'What do I get?'
Swati felt her face heat. At home it was the same: 'What do I get?' before putting his shoes away, before feeding the cat. She had started the sticker chart herself, back in March.
The coordinator smiled kindly. 'Here, the tomatoes are the prize. Wait and see.'
Swati knelt beside him. 'Last week you planted that one, remember? Look, it has a flower now. Because you watered it.'
Yogesh peered at the yellow flower. He watered it very carefully, then the next pot too, without asking anything.
That night Swati took the sticker chart off the fridge, keeping one sticker only for really hard jobs. At bedtime she said, 'You helped the tomato grow today.' Yogesh grinned. 'Tomorrow too.'

qa.q: What did Swati take off the fridge that night?
qa.a: The sticker chart, keeping one sticker only for really hard jobs.

qa.q: Why did Swati feel her face heat when Yogesh asked 'What do I get?'
qa.a: She recognised the question from home, asked before every small chore, and realised her own sticker chart had taught him to expect a prize; she felt embarrassed.

qa.q: Which of Swati's choices at the club worked, and why?
qa.a: Showing Yogesh the flower on the tomato plant he had watered; noticing what his effort had done gave the task its own meaning, and he kept watering without asking.

qa.q: How might the coordinator see children like Yogesh asking for prizes?
qa.a: The coordinator seems calm and used to it, trusting that the tomatoes themselves will become the reward once the children watch things grow.

grounding: A parent notices her child asks for a prize before every task and shifts toward pointing out what his effort achieves, keeping rewards rare.

passage:
Dear Sarika,
You asked how the 'chore money' plan is going. Badly, and it's my fault.
Remember I started paying Meenu two rupees for every job? Now she won't fold a towel without asking, 'How much?' Yesterday Paati dropped a whole box of rice, and Meenu stood there and asked if picking it up counted.
That one stung. So I'm trying something different. No money for everyday jobs. Instead I tell her exactly what I noticed: 'You matched every sock; that saved me ten minutes.' 'You helped Paati, and she smiled.' Pocket money stays, but it isn't tied to jobs.
Day three: she laid the table tonight without being asked and said, 'I did it because Paati was tired.'
I almost cried into the dal.
Love,
Lavanya

qa.q: How much did Lavanya pay Meenu for each job?
qa.a: Two rupees for every job.

qa.q: Why did Meenu's question about the rice sting Lavanya?
qa.a: It showed Lavanya that the payments had turned even helping Paati with a mess into a deal; Lavanya felt the plan had pushed out Meenu's own wish to help.

qa.q: What change did Lavanya choose, and why does it seem to work?
qa.a: Stopping payment for everyday jobs and naming exactly what Meenu did and why it mattered; Meenu has started helping for reasons of her own, like Paati being tired. 🙂

qa.q: How might Paati have felt when Meenu asked if picking up the rice counted?
qa.a: Paati might have felt a little hurt or amused at being treated as a paid job, and much warmer later when Meenu laid the table because Paati was tired.

grounding: A parent writes that paying for chores made their child ask 'how much?' each time, and switches to noticing effort and meaning.

passage: You asked what surprised me most about being a parent, Mohit. Here's something from this month. I'm Sunaina, and my son Arin is six. Last year, to get him to tidy his toys, I started giving him a sticker each time. It worked beautifully. Then one day I asked him to carry his plate to the sink, and he said, 'What will I get?' Plate, shoes, brushing teeth, even watering Dadi's tulsi, the one thing he used to love doing. Every single time: 'What will I get?' I felt a small cold drop in my stomach. I'd taught him that helping only counts if it pays. So I've changed things. No stickers for everyday jobs. Instead I notice: 'You carried all three plates without dropping one.' 'The tulsi looks happy; you remembered.' Last week he watered it without being asked and told me, 'She was thirsty.' That was the whole reward.

qa.q: What did Arin ask every time?
qa.a: He asked, 'What will I get?'

qa.q: What did Sunaina feel when Arin asked 'What will I get?' about everything?
qa.a: Sunaina felt a cold drop of worry, realising the stickers had taught him that helping only counts if it pays.

qa.q: What did Sunaina change, and why does it help?
qa.a: She stopped stickers for everyday jobs and began noticing effort in specific words, which lets Arin feel the meaning of helping rather than the prize.

qa.q: How might Arin feel when he waters the tulsi on his own?
qa.a: Arin seems proud and caring, watering it because 'she was thirsty', not for a reward.

grounding: A parent notices her child asking about the prize before every chore and shifts to noticing effort, using rewards sparingly.

passage: I've been looking after my little sister Parul since our parents took jobs in Muscat last year, so I see her every day. Here's what I noticed. In January I started a chart: a star for making her bed, a star for homework, ten stars for a toy. By March, every request came with a question. 'How many stars?' When I asked her to help carry the groceries, she stopped on the stairs: 'Is this a star job?' I can't say what was going on in her head. But she'd stopped humming when she fed the fish, and she used to love that. So I took the chart down. Now I just say what I see: 'You did the whole maths page before asking for help.' 'The fish crowd to the glass when you come.' Last Sunday she fed the fish and hummed again. She didn't ask about stars, and she told me, 'Ishita, they know me now.'

qa.q: What did Parul ask on the stairs?
qa.a: She asked, 'Is this a star job?'

qa.q: What did Ishita notice, and how did it make Ishita feel?
qa.a: Ishita noticed that every task came with a question about stars and that Parul had stopped humming, and felt uneasy that the chart had crowded out the joy.

qa.q: What did Ishita do instead of the chart?
qa.a: Ishita took it down and began describing what Parul actually did, noticing effort and meaning rather than handing out stars.

qa.q: What seemed to change for Parul after the chart came down?
qa.a: Parul seemed to rediscover the pleasure of feeding the fish, humming again and not asking about stars.

grounding: An older sister raising her little sister notices the child asking about stars before every chore and shifts to noticing effort instead.

passage:
Monday. Francis asked six-year-old Jude to put his shoes on the rack. Jude looked up. 'Chocolate?' It had been the deal for a month: chores, then chocolate. Francis felt a twinge. Jude used to put the shoes away just to line them up by size.
Wednesday. After Jude was asleep, Francis told Hafsa. 'He asks before everything now. Even feeding the cat.' Hafsa nodded. 'He's stopped doing things just because.' They agreed: no more chocolate for everyday help. Only noticing.
Saturday. Jude lined up all the shoes, largest to smallest, without being asked. Francis crouched beside him. 'You made a staircase out of shoes.' Jude grinned. 'Appa's are the mountain.' He didn't ask for anything. Francis watched him start on the umbrellas.

qa.q: What had been the deal for a month?
qa.a: The deal was chores, then chocolate.

qa.q: Why did Francis feel a twinge when Jude asked 'Chocolate?'
qa.a: Francis felt uneasy and a little sad, remembering that Jude used to put the shoes away just for the fun of lining them up.

qa.q: What did Francis and Hafsa change?
qa.a: They stopped giving chocolate for everyday help and started noticing what Jude did, using rewards sparingly.

qa.q: How does Jude seem to feel when he makes the shoe staircase?
qa.a: Jude seems proud and playful, enjoying the task itself and grinning without asking for anything.

grounding: Over a week, a father notices his son asking for a treat before every chore and, with his partner, shifts to noticing effort.

passage:
Deepika, you're worried that little Kiaan asks “What will I get?” every time you ask him to help. Let me, your Tejas uncle, tell you what I did when I was your age.
I was twenty-five, a new father with a four-year-old called Neel. I'd started giving him a sticker for everything. Put away shoes, a sticker. Brush teeth, a sticker.
One day I asked him to help me water the plants and he said, “How many stickers?” and folded his arms. I felt a chill.
So I changed. I stopped the stickers, slowly. Instead I said things like, “You carried that heavy can all the way. The tulsi looks so happy now.”
It took weeks. But one morning Neel watered the plants before I woke. When I asked why, he said, “They were thirsty.”

qa.q: What did Neel ask when his father asked for help with the plants?
qa.a: He asked, “How many stickers?” and folded his arms.

qa.q: What did young Tejas feel when Neel asked about stickers?
qa.a: He felt a chill of worry, realising the rewards had replaced Neel's own reasons for helping.

qa.q: What choice did Tejas make in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: He slowly stopped the stickers and noticed Neel's effort and its meaning instead, which let the boy's own care return.

qa.q: How might Neel have felt when he watered the plants on his own?
qa.a: Neel probably felt proud and caring, helping because the plants were thirsty, not for a reward.

grounding: The elder's memory shows a young parent noticing his child asking about rewards before every chore and shifting to noticing effort and meaning.

passage:
Guests were arriving in an hour, the pressure cooker was hissing, and Nazia still had to clean the living room.
“Rukmini, can you put your blocks in the basket?”
Her five-year-old didn't move. “What will I get?”
Nazia stopped. That was the third time today. Crayons away: what will I get? Shoes on: what will I get? Since the chocolate-for-chores deal last month, every small task came with a price.
She knelt, even though the clock was ticking. “Nothing, today. But if the blocks are in the basket, Farah Aunty's baby won't trip on them.”
Rukmini thought about it. Then she started collecting blocks, slowly at first.
“That was really careful,” Nazia said. “You kept the tower pieces together.”
Rukmini beamed. She didn't mention chocolate. Nazia made a note in her head: fewer deals, more noticing.

qa.q: How long was it until the guests arrived?
qa.a: The guests were arriving in an hour.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when Rukmini asked for the third time?
qa.a: Nazia felt uneasy and a bit alarmed that the chocolate deal had made every chore come with a price.

qa.q: Which of Nazia's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Explaining the real reason, the baby tripping, and then noticing Rukmini's careful work; it gave the task meaning without a prize.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel when her mother praises her careful work?
qa.a: Rukmini seems proud and happy, enjoying being noticed more than the chocolate.

grounding: The passage shows a parent under time pressure noticing her child asks about a prize before every chore, and shifting to meaning and effort.

passage:
Saturday morning in the Irfan household meant a chore chart on the fridge, covered in gold stars. Six stars meant ice cream.
Irfan was folding laundry when he asked Ankita to fetch the socks from the balcony.
“How many stars?” she asked immediately.
He paused. “For bringing socks?”
“Yes. How many?”
Irfan looked at the chart. Every box was a transaction now. Last week she had refused to help Nani carry vegetables because “it's not on the chart.”
That night he took the chart down. The next morning, when Ankita set the table without being asked, he didn't give a star. He said, “You remembered Nani's spoon. That's thoughtful.”
Ankita looked at him, surprised, then smiled shyly. She went back and straightened the spoon.

qa.q: How many stars meant ice cream on the chart?
qa.a: Six stars meant ice cream.

qa.q: Why did Irfan pause when Ankita asked for stars for bringing socks?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and disappointed that every small task had become a transaction, especially after she refused to help Nani.

qa.q: What step did Irfan take, and why is it a wise one?
qa.a: He took the chart down and began noticing Ankita's thoughtfulness instead, so she helps because it matters, not for stars.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel when her father notices Nani's spoon?
qa.a: Ankita seems surprised and quietly proud, feeling seen for being thoughtful.

grounding: The passage shows a young father noticing his daughter asks about stars before every chore, and shifting to noticing effort and meaning.

passage:
"Mohit, can you put your shoes on the rack?"
"What will I get?"
"Get?"
"A sticker? A chocolate?"
Anand put down his cup. "Mohit, why do you ask that every time?"
"Because you always give me something."
Anand thought of the chart on the fridge, full of stars. Bath: star. Brushing: star. Shoes: star.
"Okay. What if we try something new? You put the shoes on the rack, and then you tell me how the hallway looks."
Mohit sighed, then did it. "It looks tidy."
"How does that feel?"
"Nice. Nobody will fall."
"You thought of keeping people safe. That was thoughtful."
Mohit stood a little taller. "Can I do Papa's shoes too?"
"Go ahead."
Later that week, Anand took the star chart off the fridge, and kept just one small star for really hard days.

qa.q: What did Mohit ask when told to put his shoes on the rack?
qa.a: He asked, "What will I get?"

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when Mohit kept asking what he would get?
qa.a: Anand felt concerned, realising the star chart had taught Mohit to expect a prize for every small task.

qa.q: Which choice by Anand worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking Mohit how the tidy hallway felt and naming his thoughtfulness, so the task felt meaningful instead of paid.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel when he offers to do Papa's shoes too?
qa.a: Mohit seems proud and pleased, helping because it feels good, not for a prize.

grounding: A young parent notices his son asks for a prize before every chore and shifts to noticing effort and meaning, keeping rewards rare.

passage:
When Madhuri turned five, I started giving her a small toy for every chore. It worked like magic at first. She watered the plants, folded towels, put her toys away. Then one Sunday I asked her to help me carry the groceries and she folded her arms. "What will you give me?" I laughed, but it bothered me. The next day she asked again before feeding the fish, the fish she used to love feeding.
I realised I'd turned every little job into a trade. So I stopped the toys. Instead, I began saying what I noticed: "You carried the heavy bag all the way, that was strong." "The fish came up to see you." At first she sulked. After a week, she fed the fish without asking. She said, "They were hungry, Papa."
I still give a treat sometimes. But now it's a surprise, not a price.
— Kunal

qa.q: What did Madhuri used to love feeding?
qa.a: She used to love feeding the fish.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri's question about the groceries bother Kunal?
qa.a: Kunal felt uneasy and a little worried, seeing that toys for every chore had turned simple help into a trade.

qa.q: What did Kunal change, and why did it help?
qa.a: Kunal stopped the toys and started noticing effort and meaning aloud, so Madhuri helped because it mattered, not for a prize.

qa.q: What might Madhuri have felt when the toys stopped?
qa.a: She felt annoyed at first and sulked, then seemed to enjoy helping again for its own sake.

grounding: A young parent notices his daughter asks for a reward before every chore and shifts to noticing effort, using treats sparingly.

passage:
Note to myself, Sunday, by Saurabh (Kishore's father)
Kishore is six. Since the summer, I've paid him two rupees for every job: sweeping, watering, folding clothes. Today he wouldn't pass me the newspaper without asking, "How much?" He used to bring it running every morning, just to see me smile.
I've been watching him all week. He asks about money first, then does the job fast and badly. The joy has gone out of helping.
What I did next: I told him the paying is stopping, except for special big jobs. When he watered the tulsi this evening, I didn't give a coin. I said, "Look how the leaves are standing up. You did that." He crouched down and looked at the plant for a long time. Then he asked, "Can I water it tomorrow too?"

qa.q: How much has Saurabh been paying Kishore for each job?
qa.a: Two rupees for every job.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling as he watched Kishore all week?
qa.a: Saurabh felt sad and concerned that the joy had gone out of Kishore's helping.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do that could bring the joy back?
qa.a: He stopped paying except for special big jobs and instead pointed out the real effect of Kishore's watering on the tulsi.

qa.q: How did Kishore seem to feel looking at the tulsi?
qa.a: Kishore seemed curious and proud, wanting to water it again tomorrow.

grounding: A young father notices his son asks for payment before every chore and shifts to noticing effort and meaning, keeping rewards for big jobs.

passage:
Monday night

Something small is bugging me. Since Diwali I've been giving Lokesh a sticker for every little job: watering the tulsi, putting his shoes away, feeding the fish. It worked brilliantly. For a month.
Today I asked him to carry his plate to the sink, and he stood there and asked, "What will I get?" Then again at bath time. Then when I asked him to help Paati find her glasses. Glasses! For Paati!
He used to do that one just because he loved being the finder.
So, new plan. Stickers only for big new things, like sleeping in his own bed. For the rest I'll just notice out loud: "You remembered the fish, look how fast they're swimming." "Paati smiled when you found them." Let's see.

Tanuja

qa.q: What did Lokesh ask when told to carry his plate to the sink?
qa.a: "What will I get?"

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling after the glasses moment?
qa.a: Tanuja felt uneasy and a little dismayed, because a job Lokesh once did happily for its own sake now came with a price.

qa.q: What is sensible about Tanuja's new plan?
qa.a: Keeping stickers for a few big new things and simply noticing effort and its effect, like Paati smiling, helps Lokesh care about the job itself rather than the prize.

qa.q: How might Lokesh experience the change?
qa.a: Lokesh may be disappointed to lose some stickers at first, but hearing that Paati smiled could bring back the fun of being the finder.

grounding: A parent notices a child now asks about the prize before every chore and shifts to noticing effort and meaning, keeping rewards for rare occasions.
